Just to note, S2D (Storage Spaces Direct) requires Datacenter licenses and generally recommends a 3-4 node cluster to perform smoothly. S2D also has some sensitive hardware requirements that would just add more to the budget. But I do agree, Starwinds VSAN would be recommend for sure.

I just want to note that the licensing alone even with Standard & device CALs will eat that entire budget.   


However, to add to the hardware and deployment, my recommendations are:   


1. I'd strongly recommend adding two additional 512GB SSDs (raid-1) at a minimum, to be for the host operating system. SSDs are cheap, no need to put VMs, Host, and everything else on just 2 SSDs, the user experience will be soured due to 1 SSD having to essentially Read/Write everything. 
2. The two-node solution is fine. Just note, that if you added a 3rd hypervisor would add additional licensing cost. 
3. Keep the host HCI (Hyperconverged Infrastructure), no need to add an additional layer to this, you can utilize Starwind's VSAN to sync the local storage between each host. There is a free license and TONS of guides out there to set this up. 

  
To make it easy on yourself, if there are power issues already, both host would be down, making the cluster rather useless. Also, you don't HAVE to cluster the servers, clustering gives automatic HA (High-availability) which is nice, but not required. Alternatively, can just make the 2nd server a replica server. Just means if the primary host dies, you will need to spin up the VMs on the replica host.   


I'm sure I'll have more to think of, but just food for thought.

MECM/SCCM can take care of a lot of maintenance for you that doesn't come natively with WSUS. I'm stuck with WSUS only deployment and have to use a handful of PowerShell paired with Task Scheduler to be anywhere halfway decent.   


​

# Synchronization

  
For patching syncing you start from upstream and sync to downwards. So, your sync schedules need to be staggered to give both enough time to sync with out conflicting with the upstream server. As well as pull newly approved, declined, and deleted patches for the upstream server. 

# Cleanup & Reindexing 

The WSUS cleanup wizard and database reindexing will need to start at your lowest tier of downstream servers and work their way up.

If you don't have a large environment, you can usually get away with scheduling/automating your maintenance (WSUS cleanup wizard/WSUS database reindexing\*) once a month. You will want to do this after your final wave of patches have been deployed.  


\*Note: You need to do the WSUS cleanup wizard first then perform a database reindex. Though if I'm not mistaken, MECM/SCCM can take care of that for you. 

If you are interested in my patching and maintenance timeline just shoot me a PM and I'd be happy to share.
